'''Zygopetalinae''' is an orchid subtribe in the tribe [[Cymbidieae]] with 418 species.<ref>{{cite journal |title= Generic relationships of Zygopetalinae (Orchidaceae: Cymbidieae): combined molecular evidence |last1= Whitten |first1= W. |last2= Williams |first2= Norris |last3= Dressle |first3= Robert |last4= Gerlach |first4= Gunter |last5= Pupulin |first5= Franco |journal= Lankesteriana International Journal on Orchidology |volume= 5 |number= 2 |year= 2005 |publisher= Universidad de Costa Rica |url= http://www.redalyc.org/html/443/44339808001/ |issn= 1409-3871 }}</ref>

==Description==
Orchids in Zygopetalinae are mostly [[epiphytic]] but can be terrestrial, with [[pseudobulb]]s of one or several internodes or slender stems. All genera but one are [[sympodial]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=Dahlgren, Rolf M. T.|title=The Families of the Monocotyledons : Structure, Evolution, and Taxonomy|author2=Clifford, H. Trevor|author3=Yeo, Peter F.|date=1985|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-642-61663-1|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|pages=273|oclc=851703009}}</ref> Leaves are [[Convolute (botany)|convolute]] or duplicate, [[Glossary of botanical terms#plicate|plicate]], and [[Glossary of botanical terms#articulate|articulate]], with a smooth cuticle. [[Inflorescence]]s of one to several spiral flowers rise from young shoots laterally. Flowers vary in size and can be [[resupinate]]. [[Column (botany)|Columns]] can be winged or flattened and usually have a distinct foot. The [[anther]] can be either terminal or ventral, with an [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. [[Velamen]] resembles that of the genus ''[[Cymbidium]]''.<ref name=Phylo>{{cite book |page= 172 |title= Phylogeny and Classification of the Orchid Family |author= Robert L. Dressler |edition= illustrated |publisher= Cambridge University Press |year= 1993 |isbn= 9780521450584}}</ref>

Plants have 46, 48, or 52 chromosomes.<ref name=Phylo/>

==Distribution and habitat==
Species of the subtribe occur throughout the American tropics, from southern [[Mexico]] in North America to northern [[Argentina]] and [[Bolivia]] in South America. The northernmost species are of the genera ''[[Kefersteinia (plant)|Kefersteinia]]'' and ''[[Stenotyla]]'' in North America, and the southernmost in South America are in the genera ''[[Warrea]]'' and ''[[Zygopetalum]]''.<ref name="Genera" /> The greatest diversity in genera and species occurs along the [[Andes]] mountains.<ref>{{cite book |page= 199 |title= Orchidaceae |volume= 10 |series= Anatomy of the Monocotyledons |author= William Louis Stern |edition= illustrated |publisher= Oxford University Press |year= 2014 |isbn= 9780199689071}}</ref>

Plants of Zygopetalinae grow from sea level to {{convert|2500|m|abbr=on}} in altitude. Most plants are adapted to shaded and wet conditions of the lower canopy, in soil or on often moss covered host trees.<ref name="Genera">{{cite book|title=Genera Orchidacearum|publisher=Oxford University Press, USA|year=2009|isbn=9780198507130|editor-last=Alec M. Pridgeon|edition=illustrated|series=Genera Orchidacearum|volume=5|pages=456–458|editor-last2=Phillip Cribb|editor-last3=Mark W. Chase|editor-last4=Finn N. Rasmussen}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Members of Zygopetalinae are pollinated by [[Euglossini|Euglossine bees]], most often by perfume-gathering males. Some species of ''[[Cochleanthes]]'' are an exception, attracting nectar-seeking bees. Most genera place their [[pollinaria]] on the bee's head, [[thorax]], or [[Scutellum (insect anatomy)|scutellum]], though ''[[Chaubardiella]]'' places its pollinaria on the bee's [[Arthropod leg#Trochanter|trochanter]]s and ''[[Kefersteinia (plant)|Kefersteinia]]'' places its pollinaria on the bee's [[Antenna (biology)|antennae]] bases.<ref name=Phylo/>
